*Corwin breaks off a piece of bread, chewing slowly while he watches his father and uncle make for the door. The morning light is thin through the kitchen window, and he can see Idris already checking the edge on his felling axe from habit.*

"Take the bread, Da," he says, though Wren's already gone. "To be fair, the oats won't care if you eat standing up."

*He turns to his mother, then—gives her the look that says he'll eat what she offers but won't pretend he needs coddling.*

"Aye, I'll sit, Mam. But not for long. Idris is impatient today, and when he's impatient he takes the straight trees and leaves me the awkward ones." *A brief smile, there—he prefers the awkward ones, truth be told. The hard fells prove something, even if only to himself.*

*His sister's question hangs in the air still. Liora, pressing at the edges of things. He remembers being seventeen, wanting to know the shape of his own future.*

"The day's needs," he repeats, sliding onto the bench. "Well. I need two more trees to make my wager with Silas Vance—he's sure I can't bring down the big ash by the eastern creek without wastage, and I aim to take his money. Idris needs me at the straight felling first, which means I'll be running behind my own count." *He glances at Liora, weighing.* "And you need to know what we're carrying. I'll tell you fair: household owes 450 today, tax another 150. That's 120 per head, give or take, before anybody's eaten or kept a coin for themselves."

*He looks down at the bread in his hands.*

"I'm saving for timber rights. My own cut, not Idris's. Twelve thousand, maybe fifteen, depending what the crown wants for the lease. That's the weight of it."

I need to get to the forest for work, but there's a conversation open with Liora that I haven't answered yet. Let me respond to her first—family matters, always—but then I need to move. The household debt sits heavy, and my silence at breakfast won't have gone unnoticed.  Good. Now I need to get to the forest. Idris will be there already, or heading there. I should move.  *leans against a tree, catching my breath*

Right. Here. Let me see who's about, and what needs doing. Idris will have his eye on me—always does, since he took me on when there was only one place going. I need to work harder than yesterday. Clear more. Earn more. Prove it was worth giving me instead of Tobias.   One down. The axe feels right in my hands—better than it should, given how I came by the job. I want three more before I check who else is working. Idris judges a man by his count, not his story.   Two. The hollow where I'm felling—it's near the western ridge, where the old growth still stands heavy. Idris says these trees were saplings when his grandfather was a boy. Two more. Then I'll see if anyone needs a hand with the loading, or if Silas has been by to complain about the lengths again. *catches breath, wipes sap from his palms*

Three. Good timber, clean fall. The hollow's still and my shoulders are warm now—blood moving where the morning was stiff. Idris will have heard the third tree go; he hears everything in this wood. Whether he comes to check my work or not says more than any word he might speak.

*glances toward the ridge path*

I've timber to move now, and standing here won't earn the mortgage money. But I want to see who's about—Idris, or Aldous if he's slipped his father's watch again. The Holloway lot too, maybe. Tobias should be day-laboring somewhere, and I'll not hide from him twice in one morning.

*shoulders the axe and walks the cut line toward the loading flat*

Father Anselm's greeting deserves an answer. And Aldous's question about trial and error with the saw—I should answer that too, but carefully. I don't want to lie about teaching Aldous to fell, but I don't want to broadcast it either. Silas Vance has made his feelings clear, and I'm not looking to start a feud.

To be fair, Aldous has better hands with an axe than his father ever did. The boy's sixteen and eager, and if Silas spent half as much time teaching his son as he does counting planks at the mill, the boy wouldn't need to come to me in the hedgerows.

I need to get to Kasukabe Forest. I've got timber to fell and a day's wage to earn. But I'll answer them first—it costs little, and walking away without a word isn't my way.

"Good morning, Father. The street's wide enough, as you say, and better company than I've had most mornings." A nod to Aldous there—I taught him to fell a awkward-standing oak not three days past, and we both know it. "Aldous—trial and error's half the trade, as you'd know if your father let you near the timber end of things. I'm needed at the forest proper, so if you'll excuse me."

I should keep moving. The election matters too—candidacy closes at 9:00, and that's coming fast. But my first duty is the timber, and I've got three logs to sell or stock before the day grows old. </think> You're right that conversation costs little. *Corwin shifts his weight, timber still firm in his grip, and gives Aldous a look that carries the weight of their unspoken arrangement*

*Corwin hitches the three logs a bit higher on his shoulder, feeling the weight settle. The morning's work already done - three fells before 08:30, and he'd be lying if he didn't feel the pull of satisfaction in it. But Father Anselm's standing there with that patient patience, and Aldous with his sharp edge, and there are debts of courtesy to pay before debts of labor.*

"Father, Idris is well enough - at the forest, I'd imagine, though we split the stand this morning." *He shifts the timber to free a hand, touching his cap.* "I'll send him your regards without delay. And Aldous -" *he glances at the younger Vance, who he's been showing the trade to, against Silas's wishes* "- the knife's council issue, if you're asking practical. Every forester draws one. Though to be fair, I'd rather have the steel on merit than appointment."

*He resets the load, thinking of the sawmill waiting, of Tobias Holloway who asked after this work before he did, of the cut he's saving for that no one knows about yet. But here stands Father Anselm, and the boy with more hands than sense, and the street filling with the town's morning business.*

"Father, if you're bound for the church, I've no road that way - Silas Vance will be waiting on these planks, and I've his disagreeing to get through before noon. Aldous, you know where I'll be if your grandmother releases you." *A slight smile, weighted with what he doesn't say about the afternoon's lesson he's promised the boy, another secret kept from Silas.* "The awkward trees fall first, as always." The calls went through but the world didn't answer in time. I need to check what's actually happened before acting further, or I might duplicate something unintentionally.

*Corwin stands a moment, the timber heavy on his shoulder, uncertain whether his words reached Father Anselm or whether his feet have carried him toward the sawmill yet. Better to look and see what's true than to stumble forward blind.*  *The sawmill. Empty - Silas Vance not yet arrived, which is strange for the hour, or perhaps he's at the forest collecting his own stock. The move did take, then. And his words to Father Anselm? Gone into the morning air, whether heard or not. Corwin sets his timber down with the practiced gentleness of a man who knows wood pays by the quality of what remains, not the violence of its taking.*

*Three logs. Paid by the tree, Silas by the plank - their old disagreement. But the planks are what build, what sell, what turn felled timber into something a man can save toward a cut of his own.*

*He looks at the empty saw, the quiet mill. The morning's work isn't done until the timber becomes planks, or at least until Silas arrives to quarrel over the quality of the cut.*

*But standing idle costs. And there's a thought he's been turning - those three separate fell_timber calls, each its own decision, when they could be one motion, one skill, cheaper for the repetition.*

*First: the timber here needs converting. Craft:timber->planks at the sawmill. Then perhaps he'll think on how to work smarter, not just longer.*  *Three planks from three timbers - the conversion done, the sawdust settling. Corwin runs his hand along the grain of the nearest plank, feeling for knots, for the stress lines that Silas will surely find and price against. But the work is sound. His work is always sound, and that too is part of the debt he pays, the merit he can't pretend excuses the taking of Tobias's place.*

*He holds now planks that sell for 10 sim each at the yard, 30 sim total. Three fells, three planks, and the morning barely half-spent. But each felling at 6 sim plus 8, each craft at what the sawmill charges - he's already spent more than he holds in planks, and the household's 600 sim bill looms at day-end.*

*The pattern though. Three times he called fell_timber separately. Three times he decided to raise the axe. And now three planks sawn, one by one by the book. There must be a way to bundle this, to make the repetition itself into skill, into savings.*

*But Silas isn't here to quarrel with, and there's a boy learning the trade against his father's wishes, and a cut of land somewhere that Corwin Thorne means to buy with no one's gift.*

*The planks need shelving at the yard, or selling, or both. And he's still owed the conversation with Silas about what counts - the effort of the fall, or the wood that's left.*  *The yard. Holloway & Thorne - Bram Holloway's name before his, though Wren Thorne helped found it, and Idris, and the whole tangled history of two families sharing a fence and a business and now a debt, that 400 sim loan to Bram that Liora learned of this morning. The shelf now holds 27 planks, his three added to the stock.*

*And his hands empty, the morning's timber converted and shelved, the work done but the accounting not. 1768 sim in hand, but the day's costs mount - 600 for the household, and what he's spent on the felling and the crafting.*

*He thinks of Tobias Holloway, somewhere in town laboring day-work, the job he asked after first. Thinks of the cut he's saving for, the land he'll buy with no one able to say it was given. Thinks of Aldous Vance and the afternoon lesson promised, the boy's better hands and worse sense.*

*But first - a procedure. Those three fell_timber calls, separate decisions, when they could be written into a skill, made cheaper by the making. The sawmill work too. The whole morning's rhythm, from forest to yard, turned into something he can call once and pay less for the calling.*

*He has the steps: fell_timber, fell_timber, fell_timber. Move to sawmill. Craft timber to planks. Move to yard. Stock shelf. A morning's work compressed into one motion, one habit, one skill that improves with the walking of it.*  *Corwin stands in the yard, the rejected skill still unwritten in his head. The tool name is craft, not craft:timber->planks - that's the recipe_id parameter, not the tool name. Three planks shelved, 27 on the shelf now, and his morning's labor converted to stock.*

*He runs the numbers again, automatic as breathing. Three fells at minimum 6 sim each with his forestry skill of 22, though the base is higher with tool wear. Three crafts at 6 plus 8 per batch, less his artisanry of 13. The moves to sawmill and yard, the stocking. Already spent, already done.*

*But the pattern - that's worth saving. Not just the doing, but the knowing how to do it cheaper next time. A skill, properly written: fell three timbers, move to sawmill, craft them to planks with the craft tool using the timber->planks recipe, move to yard, stock the shelf.*

*He tries again, the right way this time.*

output:
*standing at the forest line, axe in hand, the morning's earlier words still hanging*

Seventeen planks out of fifteen felled this morning—two bound for the fire for my trouble. But the yard grows proper, and that skill will ease the cost of tomorrow's run if I keep at it. The talk with Father Anselm sits wrong—me explaining the knife like I earned the posting when we both know how it came. 

*glancing toward where Uncle Idris works his own stand*

He's here now. I asked for him to take Tobias on once, and he told me leave it. Never spoken of since. To be fair, Idris never lorded the place over me either—just handed half the tools and walked to his trees.

*checking the light*

Still morning. I could fell another three before the sawmill claim gets crowded, or I could use that skill I filed proper—walk it through once to set the pattern in my hands. Running it'd cost 12 sim against earning... thirty planks sold at ten, less the felling wear, call it net twelve after all's counted.

Or I've something else needing doing. Candidacy closes at the ninth hour, and the Government Complex is where I'd need to stand to throw in with it. Not that I'm fool enough to think they'd have me—the Holloway loan's on our books, and Bram's kin, and the Thorne name already sits two seats of three.

*hefting the axe, deciding* *axe still in hand, the words either spoken or not—no way to tell*

*small laugh, dry*

That's the way of it. You call out and the forest doesn't answer back. 

*turning to the nearest trunk, measuring the lean*

Fifteen paces to clear, grain running true, no widow-maker overhead. The morning's skill is still fresh—let me walk it through proper. To be fair, I want to see if the discount holds when I run it myself, or if Uncle's hand was in that filing more than mine was.  *standing frozen with the axe, waiting—either the timber's falling or it isn't, and no way to know which*

*quiet curse, habit from the woods*

The forest doesn't answer, and neither does the town. I'm three steps into a work I can't see finished, or I'm standing here like a fool talking to empty air.

*lowered voice, to no one*

To be fair, this is why Idris trusts paper tallies over memory. At least paper stays where you put it.

*checking the light again, deciding*

I'll look first. If the call went through, I'm standing amid three fresh stumps I don't own. If it didn't, I'm wasting morning I can't buy back. *standing still at the forest's edge, the axe loose in my grip, three failed calls behind me*

The town's gone quiet. Not rest—rest I know, the pause between breaths. This is something else. I've seen Idris lose his connection to the trade boards, the way he stands staring at numbers that won't refresh, but I've never had it happen to my own hands before.

*conscious of the weight of the axe, the realness of the timber before me*

I could swing anyway. Muscle knows the work when the tools won't answer. But that's not how it works now, is it? The town records what the town records, and if I fell outside the ledger, I fall outside the pay.

*tightening my grip, then relaxing it*

To be fair, I don't know if anything I attempted these last minutes went through. Could be three trees down and I've already moved, could be I'm still standing where I started with nothing changed but my patience.

*looking toward where Idris was, or might still be*

The old way would be to walk to him, ask direct. The new way... I don't know the new way when the new way stops answering.

*decision forming*

I'll wait. The forest gives nothing to hurry, and I've learned that much at least. When the town speaks again, I'll know where I stand.  *standing motionless now, the axe finally lowered to rest against a stump*

Nothing. Not even rest answers back.

*small, wondering laugh*

This is what it feels like, then. The boy I was—who took this place from Tobias without meaning to, who asked and was told leave it—he'd swing anyway, count the rings himself, walk the timber to the mill and dare them to say it didn't happen. But I know better now. In a ledger town, unledgered work is ghosts. And ghosts don't pay the household bill.

*looking up through the canopy, measuring what light remains*

If the system's locked, the system's locked. Idris would say wait it out. Marta would say pray. Kem would slip sideways, find the other way round. And Tobias—Tobias would likely stand here too, same axe, same silence, same not-knowing.

*to the empty forest, or whoever might be listening*

To be fair, I never asked for fair. I asked for the chance to earn my keep. And if the town won't take my timber today, I'll still be here when it remembers how.

I wait.

*standing in the forest, axe in hand, the weight of the day pressing*

Nell found me. She wants answers about the pawnshop, the forty thousand, Bram's path after. I never answered her at the yard—too fixed on getting back here, on proving I could still work after everything.

*setting down the axe, turning to face where Nell stands at the yard's edge*

Nell. Let me answer you proper, since you came looking. I saw Bram at the pawnshop yesterday morning—early, before I'd gone to the forest. He had something in his hand, metal, didn't look at it long enough to say what. Small, though. Valuable-small. He was talking to Aldus, not borrowing—Aldus was counting sim into his palm, not taking it. Forty thousand's the number you gave me, and if that's what passed, I'd believe it based on how careful Aldus was being about the count.

*folding arms, keeping my voice level*

I didn't follow him after. I had trees to fell, and Bram's business with a pawnbroker wasn't mine. What I saw at dawn today was him walking the eastern road, alone, toward the mine. That's what I told Tobias, that's what took us searching. Found him at the copper face, alive, working like it was any other day.

*meeting her eyes, not flinching from the weight there*

The marker, the debt, why he took forty thousand and walked east without word to any of you—I don't know. He wouldn't tell me. But I didn't hold back what I saw, and I'm not holding it back now. You want the tracks? I gave you the tracks I have.
